# Robert Riopel, Senior Product Designer (Canada): full site text

> The complete text of robertriopel.ca in one plain-text file, for AI assistants, search tools and anyone who prefers reading without the 3D forest. A shorter index is at https://robertriopel.ca/llms.txt.

Robert Riopel: Senior Product Designer | Product Design, Design Systems & AI Tools | Co-founder, DateNight. He is based in Canada and works in English and French (both native). He designs digital products end to end (product UX and UI for web and native mobile, design systems, growth and conversion, onboarding, internal tools, lifecycle and CRM email) and builds AI design tooling. As the sole product designer at RVezy, Canada's largest RV rental marketplace, his shipped work across the guest (B2C) and host (B2B) sides contributed $8M+ in measurable business impact and helped move the company from a $6M deficit to $1.5M EBITDA positive. In 2026 he co-founded DateNight, a dating app built around real plans instead of swiping, now in public beta in Toronto. He is open to freelance projects and to senior product design roles, in Canada or remote.

- AI Figma plugin: prompt to component
- Email builder: on-brand, no code

The trails: skills. What I do.
- Product design: End-to-end UX and UI for web and native mobile, from research to shipped, measured features.
- Growth and conversion: Checkout, onboarding and lifecycle work tied to revenue, tested and measured in GMV.
- Design systems: Token-based systems built in code first, mirrored in Figma, so design and engineering never drift.

The campfire: contact. "Building something, or hiring? Either way, I'd like to hear about it. I'm open to freelance projects and full-time roles."

## 3. About

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/about.html

Robert Riopel. Senior Product Designer · Product Design, Design Systems & AI Tooling · Co-founder, DateNight.
- Location: Canada
- Languages: English and French, both native
- Open to: freelance projects and full-time roles

I was the sole designer at Canada's largest RV rental marketplace, where I owned everything visual: product UX, UI, design systems, lifecycle campaigns, marketing, and brand.

Over three years there, my work contributed $8M+ in measurable business impact, helping the company move from a $6M deficit to $1.5M EBITDA positive.

I mentored two design interns, in the summers of 2025 and 2026, and I remain a reference for both.

I also build tools. I wrote an AI-powered Figma plugin that generates on-brand components from natural language, synced 1:1 with the coded Tailwind design system. Before that, I built the design system itself using OKLCH color tokens, Vue components, shared typography and spacing scales.

I studied Graphic Design (Advanced Diploma), earned a Bachelor of Design, and am now studying for an MSc in Technical Management, which pairs a designer's eye with how technology products are planned, built, and run.

On my own time, I ship side projects. Most recently DateNight, a dating app built around real plans instead of swiping. I co-founded it in 2026 and built it as a Next.js and React web app, now in public beta in Toronto. I also make AI-generated video campaigns. I learn by building.

I'm based in Canada and I work in English and French. I'm open to freelance projects and to senior product design roles, in Canada or remote, especially with product teams that care about measurable outcomes.

How I work:
- Design and craft: Figma, prototyping, interaction design, visual systems, responsive web and native mobile, illustration, motion.
- Strategy and growth: conversion optimization, A/B testing, lifecycle design, SEO, data-informed iteration, stakeholder alignment.
- Technology and AI: Figma plugins, Claude API, Claude Code, Next.js, React, React Native, Tailwind CSS, Vue.js, Supabase, AI-assisted design workflows.
- Leadership: cross-functional collaboration, design ops, mentoring design interns, executive presentations, roadmap influence.

Let's talk about building something that matters. Open to freelance projects, full-time roles, AI tooling, or simply an interesting problem. Email: rriopel.design@gmail.com

Systems and AI tooling

Growth and marketing design
- Email Builder (2025 to 2026): Designed and built a block-based email builder for RVezy's marketing team, enabling anyone to create on-brand, production-ready emails without engineering support. No Figma, no code; live tool.

## 5. Case study: Pay-in-Full Pricing

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/case-studies/pay-in-full.html

A new checkout option at RVezy that lets guests pay everything upfront at a discount, turning price-sensitive browsers into confirmed bookings. 2025.

- Results: +$1M in GMV in month one (incremental, measured against the split-payment control); $4M by the end of Q1 2026; 40% of eligible bookings chose pay-in-full in the first month; 0 payment-related support tickets in the first 30 days.
- Role: Sole Product Designer
- Team: PM, payments engineers, finance, legal, data analyst
- Timeline: 5-week design sprint
- Platforms: web and mobile checkout

The bet: average order value is around $1,800, normally split into a deposit and a later balance. Some guests wanted one payment and done. Offer a small discount (3 to 5%) for paying in full: guests get a price break and peace of mind, the business gets immediate cash flow, hosts get faster payouts. The challenge was complexity: deposits, insurance add-ons, damage protection, service fees and cancellation policies all interact with a third payment path.

Design decisions:
- Show the savings, not the math. A full breakdown felt like a negotiation in testing; the final design shows the discounted price with a simple "You save $X" line.
- Default to split, upsell full. A higher-looking upfront price increased abandonment for budget guests, so split payment stays the default with pay-in-full highlighted as an alternative.
- Cancel gracefully. With legal and engineering, a refund flow that refunds the actual amount paid, proportional to the cancellation policy.
- Host-side transparency. Hosts see that a guest paid in full, and their payout timeline reflects it.

The sprint: week 1 mapped every way money moves through a booking with engineering and finance; week 2 prototyped options; week 3 tested with guests; weeks 4 and 5 covered edge cases (cancellations, modifications, payout timing) and handoff.

Guest research: guests who paid early tended to book further ahead and for longer trips; families planning summer trips liked having it paid and off their minds. Pay-in-full was positioned as peace of mind with a reward attached.

After launch: launched to a portion of traffic first, watching adoption, checkout conversion and payment-related support contacts. The worry was cannibalization; measured against the split-payment control, the GMV was genuinely incremental. As the highlighted alternative rather than the default, it still won 40% of eligible bookings. Next: personalize the offer for longer or higher-value trips and test discount size.

---

## 6. Case study: Host Dashboard Redesign

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/case-studies/host-dashboard.html

Replacing a static host landing screen at RVezy with an action-driven notification centre that surfaces what hosts need to do right now, how they're performing against targets, and what's coming next. 2024.

- Results: +22% host dashboard engagement (weekly active hosts, indexed 122 vs. 100 for control); $1.5M incremental GMV attributed to faster booking acceptance; 31% fewer "what do I do next?" support tickets.
- Role: Sole Product Designer
- Scope: mobile-first dashboard, notification cards, performance benchmarks, multi-state logic
- Team: 1 PM, 3 engineers, 1 data analyst
- Validation: 50/50 A/B test, split by user ID, tracked per platform (iOS and Android)

Context: the old home screen showed a booking count and an earnings total but gave hosts no indication of what to do next. Booking requests went unaccepted, enquiries sat unanswered, and new hosts stalled mid-onboarding. Hosts also had no visibility into quality targets: 70% acceptance rate, 90% response rate (replies within 24 hours), and at most 1 cancellation per year.

What was designed: a feed of contextual notification cards, modeled on Airbnb's host home but tailored to RV rentals (inspection windows, onboarding calls, seasonal availability, multi-day trips): booking action cards, onboarding nudges, inspection reminders and opportunity cards. Designed for three states: a draft listing, published with no data, and published with data.

After launch: the 50/50 test measured acceptance rate, response rate, onboarding completion and overall engagement. It gave the team a clean answer instead of a debate and made the next round of dashboard work easier to prioritize. In a two-sided marketplace, the most valuable screen is the one that tells people what to do next. Next steps: rank cards by predicted impact per host, and turn the benchmarks into a progression system toward top-host status.

---

## 7. Case study: Host Onboarding Overhaul

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/case-studies/host-onboarding.html

Rebuilding an almost 30-step host flow at RVezy, from landing page to first listing approval, reducing friction at every step and establishing the onboarding framework still in use today.

- Results: +27% visitor-to-published-listing activation rate; an estimated $3.4M in annual booking revenue from incremental new host listings; 2.3x first-month booking rate for hosts who used smart pricing; landing page to sign-up conversion from 34% to 52%.
- Role: Sole Product Designer
- Team: PM, growth marketing, web and mobile engineers, data analyst
- Timeline: 10 months, 2022 to 2023
- Platforms: web, iOS and Android

The problem: from landing page to an approved first listing, a new host faced almost 30 steps. Of everyone who landed on the host page, 34% started sign-up, 18% reached the listing form and 9% published a listing: 91% never published. The biggest drops were at the initial value proposition and the listing creation form, which had too many required fields, confusing photo requirements and unclear pricing guidance.

What shipped:
- Reframed the landing page with a calculator-led experience: visitors enter their RV type and location to see projected earnings before creating an account. Landing page to sign-up conversion went from 34% to 52%.
- Progressive listing creation. The old form asked for 28 fields on one page. It became a guided, step-by-step flow. Required fields dropped from 28 to 12 for the minimum viable listing.
- Smart pricing guidance, photo guidance, and save and resume.

Approach: instrumented the full funnel with the data analyst, interviewed hosts who had abandoned a listing, and shipped in phases behind feature flags, each A/B tested against the old experience.

After launch: each phase was measured against a control group, which separated the effect of the design from seasonality and marketing. A minimum viable listing first and a complete listing over time worked because it was paired with persistent reminders; those reminders later grew into the onboarding cards in the Host Dashboard redesign, and the framework is still in use today. Next: personalize the flow by RV type and bring the earnings calculator into retargeting emails.

---

## 8. Case study: Roadside Assistance Portal

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/case-studies/roadside-portal.html

Helped rebuild the portal RVezy's 24/7 roadside partner used, so their agents could see each booking's coverage instead of calling us to ask. 2022 to 2023, early in Robert's time at RVezy.

- Role: led roadside operations; designed and shipped the fix
- Scope: roadside dashboard in the internal ops system, partner permissions
- Team: Robert and one engineer, who reviewed the code and kept the backend in sync
- Partner: Access Roadside, a Canadian company providing 24/7 roadside coverage

Context: RVezy partners with Access Roadside. Their agents handled RVezy cases through a portal connected to the internal operations dashboard.

Problem: constant disputes over what was covered. Coverage depended on the insurance tier each renter chose at booking: tire replacement, for example, was covered on some bookings and not others. The portal didn't show which tier applied to the booking an agent was working on, so every unclear case became a phone call.

Research: leading roadside operations, Robert handled cases directly with renters broken down on the side of the road, and Access Roadside's service providers called his cell about specific cases. Most calls weren't about the repair; they were about whether that booking covered it. Over 50% of roadside cases had some sort of dispute where Customer Success (Robert) had to get involved.

The decision, from a guide to the actual data: the first instinct was a clearer coverage guide (a PDF or FAQ explaining each tier). But agents already understood the tiers in general. What they lacked was which tier this booking had. So the fix moved from writing a guide to showing each booking's coverage in the portal.

Solution: a new dashboard for the roadside team inside the internal ops system, and revised permissions so Access Roadside agents could see each booking's specific coverage without reaching the rest of the system.

Design constraints: internal tools followed an existing Google-based style guide, so this wasn't a visual redesign. The design work was information hierarchy: what an agent needs to see first, with a renter stranded at the roadside, to make a coverage call without phoning us.

After launch: back-and-forth between Customer Success and roadside dropped significantly; contact between the two teams was cut in half. Billing stayed manual: Access Roadside emailed an invoice for every ticket.

What he'd do differently: fix billing at the same time, with a way for Access Roadside to submit invoices into the system and for finance to review them there. He raised it, others did too, and engineering built it after he'd moved off the team.

---

## 9. Case study: AI Figma Plugin

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/case-studies/ai-figma-plugin.html

A Figma plugin that uses the Claude API to generate native Figma components from prompts, synced 1:1 with RVezy's coded design system. Designed and developed by Robert. 2025.

- Role: designer and developer
- Users: mostly PMs and engineers, plus senior stakeholders who were less fluent with technical tools
- Stack: Figma Plugin API, TypeScript, Claude API
- Results: design-to-dev handoff time cut in half; 90+ components in the registry with full metadata; 3 modes (Pick, Quick Create and Variants)

How it's built: each prompt is sent to the Claude API with the full component registry as context. Claude replies with structured JSON that maps directly to Figma plugin API calls (createFrame, createText, setFills); the plugin validates the response against the registry, then builds native, editable Figma layers with correct colors, type, spacing and auto-layout. The registry is derived from the same Tailwind config that powers production, so when the coded system changes, the next generation changes with it. That is the 1:1 sync.

Obstacles: invented components and colors (mostly solved by constraining generation to the registry and validating every response), Figma API realities (font loading, programmatic auto-layout), and keeping the registry current.

After launch: introduced through live demos on real backlog requests, then office hours and a running list of failed prompts. Each failure pointed to a gap in the registry, a missing variant or an unclear instruction, and fixing them improved the plugin and the design system at the same time. Anything headed for production still went through design review.

What he learned: as the only designer, his leverage comes less from the screens he makes and more from the systems that let other people make good decisions without him.

---

## 10. Case study: Lifecycle and Email Campaigns

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/case-studies/lifecycle-campaigns.html

Designing the full email lifecycle at RVezy, from welcome sequences to re-engagement campaigns, building scalable templates in Braze and a visual language that drove measurable retention. 2022 to 2024.

- Results: +13% overall email engagement; $1.2M incremental GMV attributed to lifecycle campaigns (measured with holdout groups); 4x faster campaign production with the template system; 50+ campaign designs.
- Role: Sole designer (lifecycle, brand and product)
- Team: CRM manager, lifecycle marketer, data analyst, front-end developer
- Tools: Figma, Braze, HTML email

Scope: every customer-facing email. The designs became a modular template system in Braze: 12 reusable blocks, each tested across 30+ email clients with dark mode variants. Lifecycle map: 23 email touchpoints on the guest side and 18 on the host side; the highest-leverage moments were the 48 hours after a search without booking, the day before a trip, and a host's first week after going live. Measurement moved from open rates to clicks, bookings and GMV per campaign, with holdout groups on key flows.

---

## 11. Case study: DateNight

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/case-studies/datenight.html (the app: https://datenight.online/welcome)

DateNight is a dating app built around real plans instead of swiping. Robert co-founded it in 2026, then designed and built it. Tagline: "Browse. RSVP. Date. No Swiping." In public beta in Toronto.

- Role: co-founder, designer and developer
- Platform: Progressive Web App built with Next.js and React
- Stack: Supabase database; Vercel Web Analytics (cookieless) and Sentry for errors; Google Maps and Places APIs; Resend for lifecycle emails; its own design system; hosted on Vercel; built with Claude Code

The idea: people post real plans with a place and a time (a coffee, a concert, a hike). Everyone else browses those plans, RSVPs to the ones they'd actually enjoy, and the host approves who comes.

Design decision, browse and RSVP instead of swipe: swiping asks you to judge a face in a second; DateNight asks whether you'd enjoy this evening. The core unit is a plan, not a person: a date card leads with what, when and where, and the host is a small avatar. You RSVP to the plan, the host approves who joins (up to six people), chat opens 24 hours before the date, and each person gets three messages.

How he ships: daily, to staging and then production. Each change starts on its own branch, built with Claude Code and type-checked; it merges into the staging branch, which Vercel deploys to a staging site with its own Supabase database and test accounts; it's tested there in Chrome and Safari with two test accounts at once; then a pull request into main (with a schema check when the database changes) and Vercel deploys it to production. Database changes follow the same order: staging first, then production.

---

## 12. Case study: Email Builder

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/case-studies/email-builder.html
Live demo: https://rvezy-email-builder.vercel.app/

An internal tool Robert designed and built in a few days for RVezy's marketing team (2025 to 2026). Pick an email template, edit it in one place, preview it in light and dark mode, then copy HTML that's ready for Braze. No Figma, no code.

- Role: designer and developer
- For: RVezy's marketing team
- Output: table-based HTML email for Braze

Problem: every email campaign had to go through the same cycle: design it in Figma, export the HTML with a plugin, hand it off to Braze, then fix everything that broke on the way. Four tools and three hand-offs, for every single email. The builder replaces this entire chain so anyone on the marketing team can build an on-brand, production-ready email without design or engineering support.

Design decision: blocks, not a blank canvas. A free-form editor would have moved the problem, not solved it (Braze already has one), and every email would still need a designer to double-check it. Every email is made up of blocks, each built around RVezy's existing email styles, so there's no need to think about typography, spacing, buttons or light and dark palettes. People choose the blocks, write the content, and the design takes care of itself. The hardest parts of HTML emails are built into the blocks too: table layouts, Outlook fallbacks, phone sizes and tracking links.

How an email gets built: 1) Template: start from one of eight campaigns, each with its subject line, preheader and UTM campaign filled in. 2) Blocks: add any of 17 blocks and move them up or down. 3) Edit: click any text in the preview and type; Braze Liquid personalization keeps its fallback in the preview. 4) Preview: light and dark, desktop (660 px) and phone. 5) Copy: one click copies Braze-ready HTML, with UTM tags on every button, and the draft stays saved for next time.

Templates: Welcome, Re-engagement, Booking Confirmation, Promotional, Host Acquisition, Insurance and Protection, Anniversary or Birthday, Newsletter.

Blocks (17): Layout (Hero, Overlay Hero, Split Block, Section Header); Content (Text, Cards in 1, 2 or 3 columns); Media (Image, Photo Grid); Conversion (CTA, Stats, Banner Strip); Trust (Trust Badges, Feature Rows, Info Callout, Divider).

Built for the inbox: light and dark palettes for every block; desktop and phone previews with phone styles in the exported HTML; table layouts and Outlook fallbacks; Braze Liquid tags with fallbacks (a first name falls back to "Explorer"); a UTM builder that adds source, medium, campaign and content to every button link; AI copy assist that drafts a field's copy with the subject line as context; drafts that save as you work and reopen from the Drafts panel; images hosted on RVezy's own CDN, sized for desktop and phone by every image block.

In practice: campaigns on a deadline (a weekend flash sale goes from the Promotional template to Braze in one sitting, with AI copy assist for the headline, a dark mode and phone check, and tracking already on every button); lifecycle emails that run all year (welcome, booking confirmation and anniversary emails built once with Braze personalization, saved as drafts, and updated whenever an offer changes, without a request to design or engineering); host growth (host acquisition emails use feature rows, trust badges and an info callout to explain earnings and protection the same way in every send).

Stack: Next.js and React, Tailwind CSS, table-based HTML email, Braze with Liquid personalization, AI copy assist through its own API route, a built-in UTM builder, drafts saved in Supabase as you work, hosted on Vercel. It replaced Figma, an export plugin and hand fixes. It is one of the two projects behind his essay The End of Figma; the other is the AI Figma plugin.

---

## 13. Writing: How I built the forest

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/writing/how-i-built-the-forest/ (all writing: https://robertriopel.ca/writing/)

Build notes on the homepage, published November 20, 2026. The homepage is a walk through a forest made with three.js r187 and no framework; the rest of the site is plain HTML.

- No texture files: every tree, root, lantern and creature is drawn with Canvas 2D at load time by 18 seeded painters, so the forest grows the same way on every visit. Each painter writes four greyscale layers packed into one RGBA texture: A is the silhouette mask, R the warm parts (lantern paper, windows, embers), G the green glow (fungi, veins, eyes), B the bark detail. Lighting happens in the shader, so one texture can be lit differently wherever it stands. Painting runs in background workers.
- A 2.5D diorama: painted cutouts on planes, one InstancedMesh per texture, in near, mid and far bands. Off the path, cutouts turn with your view so they never go paper-thin.
- The sky is one shader (gradient, stars, a low sun and moon, drifting cloud, three ridges of mountains and distant conifers), drawn by true view direction so it stays put in the distance. The light runs from golden afternoon to moonlit night along the walk.
- Scrolling sets where the walker is headed; the walker goes at a walking pace. Each project in the grove is a tree whose height comes from its impact.
- Wander mode: WASD or arrow keys and drag-to-look on desktop, a thumb-stick drag on touch, with a couple of easter eggs off the path.
- Complete without JavaScript; needs WebGL2; respects reduced motion; loads when the page is idle; about 170 KB gzipped including three.js.

---

## 14. Writing: The End of Figma

URL: https://robertriopel.ca/death-of-figma/ (also in the Writing section at https://robertriopel.ca/writing/the-end-of-figma/)

A researched essay by Robert Riopel on what design tools taught us, why they're disappearing, and what comes next. Updated October 2026, 12 sources.

What is Figma: launched in 2016, browser-based, real-time and collaborative. Its breakthrough was multiplayer: designers, product managers and engineers in the same file. Between 2017 and 2023, knowing Figma deeply was a career skill.

The Adobe moment: in September 2022 Adobe announced it would acquire Figma for roughly $20 billion. Facing UK and EU regulators, the companies called it off in December 2023 and Adobe paid a $1 billion termination fee, then said it had no plans to invest further in XD. Figma went public on its own at $33 a share in July 2025.

The real threat was artificial intelligence. Timeline: Figma's April 2025 survey (78% say AI significantly improves efficiency, 32% say they can rely on its output); Claude Code generally available (May 2025); Figma Make launched at Config (May 2025); Figma IPO (July 2025); "vibe coding" named Collins Dictionary's Word of the Year (November 2025); Google's "vibe design" update to Stitch and a 12% two-day drop in Figma's stock (March 2026); Anthropic launches Claude Design (April 2026); Figma shares fall 51.6% in the first half of 2026 while revenue grows 46% year over year.

Two things he shipped: the Email Builder, and the AI Figma plugin that generates Vue and Tailwind components from the design system. The brain behind the plugin is two files, a design system doc and a color registry; the plugin is just the hands.

How he works now: Figma is the last step. Language first (Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui), explore with Claude Design and Google Stitch, prove with Claude Code and v0 against the real codebase and real data, then polish in Figma.

So is design dead? The tool was never the skill. AI can generate a UI in seconds, but it cannot tell you whether that UI respects your user. In a world flooded with AI-generated interfaces, taste is becoming rarer and more valuable, not less.

Sources include CNBC, Adobe's SEC Form 8-K, The Register, Figma, Anthropic, Collins Dictionary, VentureBeat, The Motley Fool and Vercel.
